cmCourseInfo.description: This course examines the legend of Robin Hood as originally depicted in medieval folklore and ballads – and as transmitted and developed in scholarship, communal rituals, and various literary and artistic forms from the fifteenth century to the present day. Exploring works as diverse as dramas, historical novels, paintings, children’s storybooks, scholarly histories, television scripts written by blacklisted Communists, and contemporary reworkings, this course explores such themes as legend-making and definitions of subversion, rebellion, and communal identity across centuries, cultures, and art forms.
cmCourseInfo.title: Robin Hood: Legend and Legacy

courses.name: On the Move in Medieval Eurasia

primaryOrg.name: John H. Daniels Faculty of Architecture, Landscape, & Design

cmCourseInfo.description: In this age of constant global travel, it is easy both to forget how much more complicated travel was in earlier periods, and to assume that there was very little of it. In the Medieval world, people travelled for work as traders, craftsmen and warriors; they travelled for their spirit as pilgrims; they travelled as migrants and refugees. This course will introduce students to the variety of people on the move in Medieval Eurasia, their motives, and the means they used to travel.
cmCourseInfo.title: On the Move in Medieval Eurasia

primaryOrg.name: John H. Daniels Faculty of Architecture, Landscape, & Design

cmCourseInfo.description: Barbarians have caught the modern popular imagination, and they appear to be much the same: hairy warriors who destroyed civilization. The late antique period (c.300–c.600) was a time of transition and the meetings of several cultures. This course examines the so-called barbarians who entered and soon came to rule the former Roman provinces of western Europe in this period. Our particular focus is the cultural, religious, artistic, and socio-economic aspects of barbarian peoples, and how these intersected with the civilization of Rome.
cmCourseInfo.title: How to Be a Barbarian: Beard, Battles and Belief at the Dawn of the Middle Ages

cmCourseInfo.description: The idea of the ‘middle ages’ is pervasive in Western thought, but only some of what is ‘traditional’ actually happened. This course introduces various interpretations, constrictions, and re-creations. Our analysis will draw on literary texts and their various interdisciplinary interpretations and applications.
cmCourseInfo.title: Medieval Mythologies and Methodologies

notes.name: Course Note
notes.content:
Timetable Instructions

LEC0101 - God and Geometry

This course engages controversial issues in the natural sciences of importance to Christian faith, with particular emphases on their ancient and the medieval origins and enactments. Examples include: Harmony vs. Chaos, Creation vs. Evolution, Free Will vs. Determinism, Reason vs. Revelation, Miraculous vs. Natural Causation.

LEC0101 is cross-listed with CHC383H1.

LEC0201 - The Global Middle Ages

The premodern world was an interconnected network of merchandise, luxury goods, religious beliefs, philosophies, and artistic production that celebrated the staples of narrative storytelling, from brave warriors and courtly lovers to tragic histories and comedies of daily life. In this course, we will explore a broad range of medieval literature (all in modern English translation) from around the world: Europe, the Mediterranean world, Africa, and Asia. We will encounter a variety of genres, including epics, sagas, romances, fabliaux, riddles, drama, lyrics, and saints’ lives, and we will work to situate each work in its social and historical contexts with materials from libraries, museums, and art galleries both at home and abroad.

LEC0301 - Imagining the World: Maps in the Middle Ages

The history of map making, or cartography, often makes a strong distinction between the fantastical accounts of the world in pre-modern maps and the apparently accurate and technical maps of the modern era.  Maps, regardless of what period they are from, are primarily representations of how people regard the world in terms of their cultural and religious values.  In this course, we will explore how people in the Middle Ages mapped out their understanding of reality.  We will start with how they mapped the universe as a whole and then we will move to how the physical world around them was captured in illustrations and literary accounts.  We will extract from these representations the core cultural and religious values that were the engines of map design.  The course will conclude with world maps that were created for trade but also for identifying who was a friend and who was a stranger.

LEC0401 - Mystery, Forgery, and Fake News in Medieval and Early Modern Books

The history of bookmaking, from antiquity to relatively recent times, is riddled with enigmatic and mesmerizing artifacts—objects that have ignited endless debates and spilled rivers of ink. In some cases, scholars have yet to reach a universally accepted conclusion about their authenticity, their origins, or their meaning. Since control over written culture has always been a powerful tool for advancing political, ideological, and economic interests, it is hardly surprising that forgers in every age have sought to exploit it. In this course, we will come face to face with some of these extraordinary objects and figures: manuscripts, papyri, and maps that have left an indelible mark on the cultural history of Europe—and far beyond. Among them are the Donation of Constantine, a medieval parchment of enormous political consequence—tragically, and spectacularly, a forgery; the Voynich Manuscript, a book shrouded in the mystery of an undeciphered script and an unknown language that has defied every attempt at interpretation; the Vinland Map, a medieval vision of the world astonishingly ahead of its time, on which even the most advanced scientific methods have stumbled (though not philology…); the Artemidorus Papyrus, a precious document whose authenticity continues to spark fierce scholarly battles; and Constantine Simonides, a Greek forger who claimed to possess original manuscripts of Homer and the Bible. We will examine the challenges these haunting artifacts pose to scholars, explore the methods used to unravel—or fail to unravel—their secrets, and reflect more broadly on their significance for the eras in which they were (or were not) created. Ultimately, we will ask what these objects can still teach us about the world we inhabit today.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.content:
Timetable Instructions

LEC0101 - Old Saxon

Old Saxon is the language spoken by the Continental Saxons--those who did not migrate to Britain in the fifth and sixth centuries. It is closely related to Old English and Old High German, and is one of the oldest surviving Germanic languages. The principal literary monument is the Heliand, a narrative of the life of Christ based on the four gospels of the New Testament, composed in alliterative Germanic metre. This course provides an introduction to the language through reading selections of the Heliand.

LEC0201 - Windows into the Workshop: Artists and Art Practice in the Middle Ages & Renaissance

In this seminar, we will peer through the window of the workshop to better understand medieval and early modern makers, their work, and the world they inhabited. Practical aspects, such as materials, techniques, and the economics of craft will be considered in conjunction with intellectual and spiritual aspects of making as they relate to concepts of labor, perfection, and the imagination.
